sections.h2: How does a Tennessee delinquent tax suit lead to a tax sale?
sections.html:
Property taxes are due on the first Monday in October and turn delinquent on March 1 of the following year. After that, the county trustee can still collect the tax with penalty and interest, but only until the account is turned over to the delinquent tax attorney.

The attorney then files suit in chancery or circuit court after February 1 and before April 1. The complaint may name every delinquent taxpayer in the county, and the suit takes priority on the court's docket. Once a defendant pays the tax, interest, penalty and accrued court costs, the proceeding is dismissed as to that owner's property without any court order, according to the UT County Technical Assistance Service reference on the suit.

Two points from that reference matter to owners. A court has no authority to delay collection or to order payment in installments, even where more time would help the county. And a court keeps jurisdiction to collect the tax even if the assessment was wrong or the procedures were flawed, so an owner who thinks the assessment is wrong should not rely on the suit to fix it.

sections.h2: What happens at a Tennessee tax sale?
sections.html:
After judgment, the county holds a public sale of the parcel for cash, subject to the owner's equity of redemption. That term means the taxpayer can still pay the taxes, interest, penalties and costs and end the sale proceeding.

  • Advertisement: one notice in the newspaper, or printed handbills if the court orders, lists the owners, describes each parcel by deed book and page or property number, and states the amount of each judgment.
  • Mailed notice: certified return receipt mail goes to the owner's last known address in the assessor's records and to anyone else with an interest who can be found after a reasonable search.
  • Recorded notice: a version of the sale notice may be recorded with the register of deeds, for information only, with no release required.
  • Who may not buy: people with a duty to pay the taxes, fiduciaries of the taxpayer, and usually a spouse buying the other spouse's property.
  • County bid: the clerk bids the amount due if no one offers the same or more, except where the county legislative body has decided not to bid on environmentally risky or non-buildable parcels.

Sale proceeds first pay the delinquent tax attorney's compensation, then the costs of the suit, then the state, the county and the municipality in that order. If money remains, the person who got notice of the sale also gets notice of the proceeds, how they were divided and the remainder.

sections.h2: How long does a Tennessee owner have to redeem after a tax sale?
sections.html:
The right to redeem vests in all interested persons when the court enters its order confirming the sale, and it can never be exercised more than one year after that date. The redemption period for each parcel is set by the court before the sale and may be restated in the confirming order. The length depends on how long the taxes went unpaid.

A 2026 change adds a second scale. Public Chapter 971 (Senate Bill 1983 and House Bill 1932) amends Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-2701(a)(1)(C), effective July 1, 2026, and applies to orders confirming a tax sale that are entered on or after that date. That date has now passed, so any order entered since then follows the newer schedule.

Tennessee redemption periods by years of delinquency
Order confirming sale enteredYears delinquentRedemption period
Before July 1, 2026Five or fewerOne year
Before July 1, 2026More than five, fewer than eight180 days
Before July 1, 2026Eight or more90 days
On or after July 1, 2026Three or fewerOne year
On or after July 1, 2026More than three90 days

Sources: UT CTAS redemption reference (earlier scale); UT CTAS 2026 index of acts (Public Chapter 971). A vacant or abandoned property can have a thirty-day period regardless of the number of delinquent years, where the court finds a reasonable basis to believe the property is vacant, or, for vacant land, abandoned.

sections.h2: What does it cost to redeem?
sections.html:
Before filing the motion to redeem, the person redeeming pays the clerk the total delinquent taxes, penalty, interest and court costs, plus interest on the whole purchase price the buyer paid. That interest is 12 percent a year, running from the day the purchaser paid the clerk until the motion is filed. If the full amount is not paid on time, or the motion is not timely filed, the redemption fails.

  • The motion must describe the parcel, the sale date and the date of the order confirming the sale, and state why the filer has a right to redeem.
  • Within ten days after the filing and payment, the clerk sends notice to the purchaser and to everyone entitled to redeem.
  • The purchaser has thirty days after the notice is mailed to ask for additional money to cover the amounts it spent on the property.
  • Additional funds ordered by the court are due by the later of the end of the redemption period or thirty days after the order.

When redemption is completed, title is divested out of the purchaser and the clerk refunds the purchase money. The owner's interest returns to the position it held when the sale was confirmed. A lienholder who redeems may then proceed to foreclose.

sections.h2: Can a buyer purchase the right to redeem?
sections.html:
A transferee can bring a motion to redeem, but the statute guards against profiteering. The court must deny the motion if the tax sale purchaser or another interested party objects and it appears the transferee is speculating. Speculation is presumed when the right of redemption was transferred for less than the purchase price at the tax sale minus what the debtor would have paid to redeem. The court may award attorney's fees to the party who successfully challenges the motion.

This matters to an owner who is thinking of selling. A buyer who pays real money for the house itself, and who pays off the taxes, is in a different position from someone buying only a redemption right at a discount.

sections.h2: Can an owner sell the house before a Tennessee tax sale happens?
sections.html:
Yes. Until the sale, the owner holds title and can sell. Paying the tax, interest, penalty and costs ends the suit as to that parcel, so a closing that pays the balance clears the proceeding. If the account is still with the trustee, the trustee must accept the delinquent tax with penalty and interest.

  • Ask the county trustee for the current balance, or the delinquent tax attorney's office if the suit has been filed.
  • Ask the clerk of the chancery or circuit court whether a sale date has been set.
  • Give the title company the payoff figure so it can be paid at closing.

After the sale, a different timeline controls. The owner's interest is subject to the redemption period, and a sale of the house during that window has to deal with the purchaser's position and the clerk's records. An attorney can sequence that step.

faqs.q: When do Tennessee property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: On March 1 of the year after the first Monday in October due date, according to the UT County Technical Assistance Service. The trustee keeps accepting payment with penalty and interest until the account goes to the delinquent tax attorney.

faqs.q: When is the delinquent tax suit filed?
faqs.a: After February 1 and before April 1, in chancery or circuit court, by the delinquent tax attorney.

faqs.q: What is the interest rate to redeem a property sold at tax sale?
faqs.a: Twelve percent a year on the purchaser's full purchase price, from the day the purchaser pays the clerk until the motion to redeem is filed, plus the delinquent taxes, penalty, interest and court costs.

faqs.q: How long is the redemption period for a sale confirmed in 2026?
faqs.a: For orders confirming a sale on or after July 1, 2026, it is one year if the delinquency was three years or less and 90 days if it was longer, under Public Chapter 971. A vacant or abandoned property can have a 30-day period.

faqs.q: Who gets the money left over after a Tennessee tax sale?
faqs.a: Proceeds pay the attorney, then costs, then the state, county and municipality. If anything remains, notice of the remainder goes to the person who received the sale notice, as CTAS describes the process.
